eye.e: From Middle English e, eye, eyghe, eyȝe, eȝhe, iȝe, ye, yhe, from Old English ēage, ēge (“eye”), from Proto-West Germanic *augā, from Proto-Germanic *augô (“eye”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Other Indo-European cognates include Breton eneb (“inverse; face; honour”), Cornish enep (“face; exterior.
eye.g: An organ through which animals see (“perceive surroundings via light”).

eye.e: Probably from rebracketing of a nye as an eye.

eyebrow.e: From Middle English eȝebreu, alteration of Old English ēaganbrū (“eyebrow”), equivalent to eye + brow. The corresponding Old English ēagbrǣw meant "eyelid".
eyebrow.g: The hair that grows over the bone ridge above the eye socket.

eyed.e: From Middle English eyed, eied, iȝed, y-yȝed, equivalent to eye + -ed.

eyelid.e: From Middle English eyelidd, eye-led, eiȝelid, eghe-lydd, yȝe-lydd, ehlid, yhelidd, from an unrecorded Old English *ēaghlid (“eyelid”), from Proto-West Germanic *augahlid (“eyelid”), equivalent to eye + lid. Generally superseded non-native Middle English palpebre (“eyelid”), borrowed from Latin palpebra (“eyelid”) (see Modern English palpebra).
eyelid.g: A thin skin membrane that covers and moves over an eye.

eyesalve.e: From Middle English eȝhe-salfe, from Old English ēagsealf (“eye-salve”), from Proto-West Germanic *augasalbā (“eye-salve”), equivalent to eye + salve.

eyeservice.e: From eye + service, by analogy with lipservice.
eyeservice.g: Work or service done only when one's employer is watching; service done for show.

eyesight.e: From Middle English eiȝesiht, ieȝesihte, ehsihthe, eihsihthe, eȝhesihthe, equivalent to eye + sight.
eyesight.g: Vision or the faculty of sight.

eyewitness.g: Someone who sees an event and can report or testify about it.
